Comprising No. 1 and No. 2 Squadrons flying Beaufort light bombers, No. 31 Squadron with Beaufighter long-range fighters, and No. 18 (Netherlands East Indies) Squadron operating B-25 Mitchell medium bombers, the wing played a pivotal role in Allied air operations across the South West Pacific during World War II. From March to April 1944, it conducted sustained attacks on Japanese shipping and installations in Timor in support of Operations Reckless and Persecution—the amphibious landings at Hollandia and Aitape—significantly weakening enemy defenses. Notably, a major raid on Su in Dutch Timor on 19 April destroyed key infrastructure and earned commendation from Air Vice Marshal "King" Cole, while a daylight strike on Dili in Portuguese Timor coincided with the invasion day, contributing to the minimal resistance encountered.

Throughout mid-1944, the wing intensified its campaign, with Nos. 1, 18, and 31 Squadrons striking Japanese positions in Timor despite challenges such as limited targets and inadequate forward airfields. No. 2 Squadron transitioned to Mitchell bombers and returned to action by June, while No. 18 Squadron flew 149 sorties that month, damaging enemy airfields and shipping, though suffering the loss of its commanding officer. The wing also supported the Noemfoor operation, with No. 18 Squadron emerging as its most active unit, flying 107 sorties. However, subsequent raids on Ceram and Celebes in September incurred heavy losses—nine aircraft and twenty-six crewmen, including Squadron Leader Wilbur Wackett—prompting a temporary suspension of Mitchell operations for crew retraining.

Preparations began to move the Mitchell force to Jacquinot Bay in New Britain, culminating in a significant joint mission on 6 April when all twenty available Mitchells joined No. 82 Wing’s Liberators in attacking a Japanese convoy including the cruiser *Isuzu*. Despite the Liberators’ delay, the Mitchells pressed on alone at the edge of their range, successfully scoring two direct hits under intense fire without loss; the damaged *Isuzu* was later finished off by Allied submarines.

In May 1945, plans to base the wing in New Britain were cancelled due to Dutch requests for air support over the Netherlands East Indies. Following the Soviet occupation of Romania in 1944–45, the Romanian Land Forces (RLF) underwent a comprehensive reorganization under Red Army supervision, marking the beginning of a deep structural and ideological transformation. Pro-German elements were purged, and two volunteer divisions—Tudor Vladimirescu First Volunteer Division and Horia, Cloșca și Crișan Division—formed from Romanian ex-prisoners of war and Communist activists in the USSR, became the foundation of the new Soviet-aligned military. The RLF’s organizational structure evolved significantly over the decades. Initially divided into three military regions headquartered in Cluj-Napoca, Bacău, and Bucharest—each convertible into army corps during wartime—this system was replaced on 1 July 1947 by the establishment of the 3rd Military Region from the former Fourth Army. By 30 April 1960, military regions were abolished and transformed into standing armies, culminating in the creation of four armies by 5 April 1980, with headquarters in Bucharest (First Army), Buzău (Second Army), Craiova (Third Army), and Napoca (Fourth Army). Surface-to-surface missile battalions operated 30 FROG-3 and 18 SCUD launchers, organized into batteries with single launchers each. Although the FROG-3 was outdated and inaccurate for conventional use, both systems had strategic potential when armed with nuclear or chemical warheads. Notably, a former Romanian official revealed in 1988 that Romania had produced chemical agents suitable for delivery via these missiles, underscoring the country’s capacity for weapons of mass destruction despite its nominal alignment within the Warsaw Pact framework. This combination of Soviet-inspired organization, large-scale conscription, and advanced fire support systems defined the RLF as a formidable, ideologically controlled force throughout the Cold War era.
